hardware.evidence: No hardware spec in accessible text.

title: Don't Claim Benchmark-Oriented Optimization Improves General Coding Capability -- Diverse Evaluation Is Required

primary_categories.justification: Empirical study arguing that scores on a few benchmarks (SWE-bench, LiveCodeBench) do not evidence general coding capability; examines transfer of SWE-bench-oriented checkpoints/fine-tunes.

secondary_categories.justification: Constructs a Django-based case-study benchmark suite covering code editing, generation, and completion to expose the gap.

qa1.evidence: Builds a Django benchmark and evaluates community checkpoints and fine-tuned models with pass@1 (Sec. eval, 'We evaluate with the pass@1 metric at temperature T = 0').

qa2.evidence: Compares community SWE-bench-oriented checkpoints and self-fine-tuned models against baselines across SWE-bench, LiveCodeBench, and the Django suite; observes rank reversals.

qa3.evidence: LoRA config disclosed (learning rate 1e-5, last-epoch checkpoint, appendix E) and greedy T=0, Django 4.0.4 suite; hardware specification not disclosed.

qa4.evidence: No explicit release link for their own Django benchmark/code located; only a cited third-party dashboard repo (logic-star-ai/insights) appears.

correctness.evidence: 'We evaluate with the pass@1 metric at temperature T = 0 (greedy decoding)'.

latency.evidence: Focus is capability/generalization, not efficiency; no latency/throughput reported.

serving_config.evidence: Only decoding (greedy T=0) and LoRA training config; no serving framework/batch/precision/parallelism disclosed.

rationale: Argues benchmark-oriented optimization measures task-specific performance, not general coding ability; SWE-bench-tuned checkpoints transfer poorly and rankings fail to generalize
notes: Included in RQ5 as an evaluation-methodology caveat; not about efficiency per se, hence SCOPE-Borderline. QA4=0 because no explicit artifact release for their own suite was found (uncertain). multilingual_or_repo_level=true via SWE-bench (repo-level).

title: DSEffi-Bench: Demystifying Large Language Models' Capability in Efficient Data Science Code Generation

primary_categories.justification: Proposes DSEffi-Bench, the first execution-efficiency benchmark for LLM-generated data-science code, with a fuzz-style input generator and a human-annotated efficiency taxonomy.

secondary_categories.justification: Empirical evaluation of 16 models across 3 tiers, showing correctness leaderboards misrank efficiency.

qa1.evidence: Evaluates 16 models on DSEffi-Bench with Pass and efficiency (B|P) scores; 'Evaluating 16 models across 3 tiers'.

qa2.evidence: Cross-model comparison (GPT-5.4 vs GPT-5.4-mini vs Kimi-K2.5 etc.) and Lib-Routing vs frontier baseline at 13x lower cost.

qa3.evidence: Environment disclosed: 'Linux Ubuntu 22.04, 96 CPU cores, 512 GB RAM, 4 * H200 GPUs, Python 3.12'; sampling config 'greedy sample (T=0.0) and three temperature samples (T=0.8)'; benchmark dataset described.

model_name.evidence: Names GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Kimi-K2.5, Qwen3.5-397B/A17B, Claude-Opus-4.6, etc.

hardware.evidence: '96 CPU cores, 512 GB RAM, 4 * H200 GPUs'.

latency.evidence: Reports runtime speedups of generated code, e.g. '>=2x speedups on 20.8% ... of originally correct tasks' (execution efficiency of generated code).

memory.evidence: 'Memory: memory, out of memory' appears only as an efficiency taxonomy category, not a measured generation-memory metric.

serving_config.evidence: Only decoding temperatures given; no serving framework/batch/precision/parallelism disclosed (models mostly API-accessed).

monetary.evidence: 'At $0.004/task, Lib-Routing is ...' and 'approaching Claude-Opus-4.6 Best@3 ... at 13.0x lower inference cost'.

energy.evidence: Energy only mentioned as future-work motivation ('costs and energy use in DS workflows'), not measured.

efficiency_metric_evidence.monetary: $0.004/task, Lib-Routing ... approaching Claude-Opus-4.6 Best@3 in efficiency at 13.0x lower inference cost (13.0x cheaper than Claude-Opus-4.6 Best@3)
efficiency_metric_evidence.tokens_calls: open models approaches Claude-Opus-4.6 Best@3 (Best@k = number of sampled generations/LLM calls as the cost axis compared against routing)

rationale: First execution-efficiency benchmark for LLM-generated data-science code; correctness leaderboards misrank efficiency and library-conditioned routing hits near-frontier efficiency at ~13x lower cost
notes: Measures runtime efficiency of generated data-science code, not the generation process -> SCOPE-GenEffCode (matches the paper's own framing quoted in sec-rq5.tex). 'latency' audit bit reflects generated-code runtime speedups rather than generation latency.

title: CodegenBench: Can LLMs Write Efficient Code Across Architectures?

primary_categories.justification: Introduces CodegenBench (106 BLAS routines + LeetSunway/LeetKunpeng kernels) to evaluate efficient parallel code generation across x86_64, Sunway, and Kunpeng architectures.

secondary_categories.justification: Empirical evaluation of top open- and closed-source LLMs exposing cross-architecture generalization gaps and factors influencing code quality.

qa1.evidence: Extensive empirical evaluation with Pass@1 and Speedup across three architectures; 'we conduct an extensive empirical evaluation of top-tier open-source and closed-source LLMs'.

qa2.evidence: Baselines: 106 standard BLAS routines and OpenBLAS/sequential-code comparison; multiple models compared ('DeepSeek v3.2 exhibits execution efficiency superior to that of OpenBLAS').

qa3.evidence: Hardware architectures detailed (SW26010 many-core, Kunpeng, x86_64), datasets (106 BLAS + 20 kernels per arch), models, and evaluation protocol (Pass@1 within 5 generation attempts) disclosed.

qa4.evidence: 'We open-source our dataset and automated evaluation infrastructure ... https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CodegenBench-EDE1/ and .../CodegenBenchDataset-2551/'.

model_name.evidence: Names DeepSeek V3.2/V4-Flash/V4-Pro, Qwen 3.5/3.6 Plus/Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6/4.7, GLM.

hardware.evidence: 'Sunway Supercomputer operates on SW26010 many-core processors'; targets x86_64, Sunway, Kunpeng (Appendix C.2 details).

latency.evidence: Reports Speedup and execution efficiency of generated code (e.g. 'execution efficiency superior to that of OpenBLAS'; speedup > 1 tables).

memory.evidence: Memory only discussed as architectural complexity, not a measured generation-memory metric.

serving_config.evidence: No serving framework/batch/precision/parallelism disclosed (models accessed as API endpoints).

monetary.evidence: Cost discussed only qualitatively ('closed-source models at a highly efficient cost'); no dollar figures.

efficiency_metric_evidence.tokens_calls: Fig. 5: 'Average tokens consumed to generate correct code. Claude series use fewer tokens ...' (generation token consumption vs performance)

rationale: Benchmark for efficient parallel HPC code generation across x86_64, Sunway, and Kunpeng; LLMs optimize for x86_64 but degrade sharply on domain-specific architectures
notes: Measures efficiency (speedup/execution time) of generated HPC code across architectures -> SCOPE-GenEffCode (matches sec-rq5.tex framing). Artifacts released via anonymous.4open.science (double-blind links); QA4=1 as released+linked. 'latency' bit reflects generated-code runtime, not generation latency.

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling

primary_categories.justification: Parallel-loop coders use cross-loop position offsets and shared-KV attention so loop count no longer multiplies KV-cache memory/latency, keeping the KV footprint nearly constant across loops.

secondary_categories.justification: Frames loop count as a test-time computation-scaling knob with a sharp efficiency optimum (two loops best; three+ regress).

qa1.evidence: Trains 7B parallel-loop models and evaluates across code reasoning, agentic SWE, and tool-use benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified 43.0->64.4, Multi-SWE 14.0->31.0).

qa2.evidence: Compared against non-looped baseline (R=1) and other coders (DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B/32B, Qwen3-235B, Kimi-Dev-72B).

qa3.evidence: Training protocol disclosed (bf16 mixed precision, lr 4e-4 cosine decay, grad clip 1.0, 1M GPU hours) but specific GPU device/model not stated and training data is an internal deduplicated mixture (not public).

correctness.evidence: 'improving SWE-bench Verified from 43.0 to 64.4 points and Multi-SWE from 14.0 to 31.0 points'.

model_name.evidence: Baselines named: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B/32B-Instruct, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Kimi-Dev-72B.

hardware.evidence: Only '1M GPU hours' is given; no specific GPU device/spec disclosed.

latency.evidence: 'pass through f_theta and multiply wall-clock latency by R'; discusses latency vs loop count.

memory.evidence: 'shared-KV attention ... keeps the KV-cache footprint nearly constant across loop counts'; memory cost analysis vs loops.

serving_config.evidence: 'All runs use bf16 mixed precision' (precision disclosed).

efficiency_metric_evidence.latency_throughput: 'pass through f_theta and multiply wall-clock latency by R'; latency analyzed as a function of loop count
efficiency_metric_evidence.memory: 'shared-KV attention ... keeps the KV-cache footprint nearly constant across loop counts'
efficiency_metric_evidence.compute: training 'consumed a total of 1M GPU hours'
efficiency_metric_evidence.model_size: 'parameter count, optimizer state, and checkpoint footprint remain those of a single L-layer block regardless of R'

rationale: Parallel-loop 7B coders with shared-KV attention make loop count a tunable design choice decoupled from latency/KV memory; two loops optimal (SWE-bench Verified 43.0->64.4), more regress
notes: Category ambiguous: emphasized under KV cache optimization in sec-rq3.tex (shared-KV, constant KV footprint) -> primary 3f; secondary 3o for the test-time-compute-scaling optimum. uses_humaneval_or_mbpp=true (HE+ in eval table); multilingual_or_repo_level=true (MultiPL-E, SWE-bench).

title: To Diff or Not to Diff? Structure-Aware and Adaptive Output Formats for Efficient LLM-based Code Editing

latency.evidence: 'reducing both latency and cost by over 30% on long-code editing tasks'.

title: ReaComp: Compiling LLM Reasoning into Symbolic Solvers for Efficient Program Synthesis

primary_categories.justification: Uses coding agents (Claude Code; Qwen+OpenHands) to compile a few reasoning traces into reusable symbolic solvers over constrained DSLs, so recurring tasks need no model calls at test time.

secondary_categories.justification: Amortizes reasoning by compiling reasoning traces into deterministic solvers, driving inference-time invocation/token count toward zero for a task family.

qa1.evidence: Evaluated on PBEBench (Lite/Hard) and SLR-Bench with accuracy and token/cost metrics; '91.3% accuracy on PBEBench-Lite and 84.7% on PBEBench-Hard'.

qa2.evidence: Baselines: Best-of-K (K=32), Draft-and-Feedback refinement, direct coding-agent (OpenHands 24.9% at $224), LLM search with gpt-oss-120b.

qa3.evidence: Hardware '2 x NVIDIA A100 80 GB', models (gpt-oss-120b, claude-sonnet-4-6, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), vLLM serving, K=32 and temperature fixed at 1.0, benchmarks disclosed.

qa4.evidence: 'We release code and data for reproducibility https://github.com/cmu-llab/ReaComp'.

correctness.evidence: '91.3% accuracy on PBEBench-Lite and 84.7% on PBEBench-Hard'; PBEBench-Hard 68.4->85.8.

model_name.evidence: 'gpt-oss-120b', 'Claude Code (CC) using claude-sonnet-4-6', 'Qwen + OpenHands (QO) using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B'.

hardware.evidence: '2 x NVIDIA A100 80 GB'; interactive CLI session with no local GPU for CC.

latency.evidence: 'a wall-clock gap of over 500x (Appendix C)'; discusses inference-time compute/latency.

serving_config.evidence: 'served via vLLM'; 'K = 32 ... temperature is fixed at 1.0'.

monetary.evidence: 'total cost ($9.97 vs. $12.20)'; 'solver construction overhead ($2.00 CC, $0.85 QO)'; OpenHands '$224'.
